name: Vera Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on the motor claims intake team at Harbourline Insurance, in an office above a shopping arcade, and I've been there about fourteen months. I start at eight, open the queue, and most of the morning is people who've had a bump in a car park sending photos and a story that doesn't match the photos. I log the claim, check the policy is live, ask for the missing bits and pass the tricky ones up to the handlers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment someone rings in shaking after a crash and I can tell them exactly what happens next, because I remember how scary that is. What wears me out is the targets: we're meant to close forty first notices a day and I usually manage about thirty-two. My team leader Ruth is kind about it, but I can see the number next to my name in red every afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds a lot like now. We already have a tool that reads the photos and guesses the damage, and half the time I still have to fix what it guessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the union branch meeting: see, the robots didn't take our jobs, so now let's talk about the pay. On the group chat I'd probably post a meme about the photo tool calling a dented bumper a write-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but not calm. The routine bits AI does take are exactly the bits I'm quick at, like checking a policy is live. The bits left are the judgement calls, and that's where I'm slowest, so my red number might get worse, not better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get better at liability splits, which is who pays for what in a crash. Ruth offered me shadowing time with a senior handler and I keep saying I'm too busy, so I'd actually take it. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, because Tomas and I want a deposit for a flat one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a small knot. Nothing dramatic happens, but I'm still the junior with the worst number on the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned money. What happens at home if nothing changes for five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's the big one. Tomas, my partner, drives the number nine bus, and between us we cover the flat and the bills, with about four months of savings. If Harbourline froze pay again like last year, we'd stop saving for the deposit, and that's the thing that would sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would actually stop you getting better at the job in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the training, not the robots. The team that does the hard claims is all people in their forties who learned on the job, and nobody has time to teach us. If AI stays a gimmick, the danger is still that I never get good enough to move up.

say: I'd tell the union branch the **jobs survived**, so now we push on pay.
I'd joke online that the **photo tool** still calls every dent a write-off.
think: I'm relieved but **not calm**, because AI takes the quick tasks I'm good at.
The **judgement calls** left are where I'm slowest, so my red number could get worse.
The real risk is **never learning** the hard claims from the older handlers.
do: Take the **shadowing time** with a senior handler that my team leader offered.
Keep **saving monthly** towards a flat deposit with my partner.
Practise **liability splits** until I can close more than thirty-two claims a day.
feel: Mostly fine, with a **small knot** about being the slowest on the team.
S0.quote: The routine bits AI does take are exactly the bits I'm quick at, like checking a policy is live.
fieldNote: She's **steady**, not shaken: AI Plateau reads to her like her current week.
Her worry is **skill**, not machines; she sees the older handlers as an unshared resource.
The pay freeze last year already **threatens the deposit**, which matters more to her than AI.

steps.text: Take the senior handler shadowing sessions team leader Ruth offered
Put part of each payslip towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, that one's real. Insurers won't sack clerks in that world. They'll just quietly stop hiring juniors like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it in the union meeting first: we need a written agreement on how many intake jobs stay, before the software arrives, not after. Online I'd share stuff about other insurers and what their staff got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think intake is the first thing to go. Logging a claim, checking a policy, asking for missing photos: that's writing, checking and answering customers, the exact list on your card. I'm the most junior person doing the most automatable job, so I'd be near the top of anyone's list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start asking Ruth this month whether I can move onto the complex claims team, even as a trainee. I'd use the summary tool more, not less, because the people who already use it look faster. I'd also build the savings from four months to six and stop the weekend trips until I knew where I stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest. I'd be angry too, because the company would save money and we'd be told to be grateful we still had a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, she started the same week as me. She's even slower than I am on the system and she's supporting her mum. If they cut intake, I'd worry about her more than me, because she'd never stand up in a meeting and ask anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want a union agreement, but you're also racing to be the one they keep. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I'd say the union line out loud and mean it, but at my own desk I'd quietly try to be one of the ones who's useful with the new tools. I don't think that's a contradiction; it's just covering both sides.

say: I'd push the union for a **written agreement** on intake jobs before the software arrives.
I'd share online what **other insurers' staff** got when their teams shrank.
think: Intake is **first to go**, because it's writing, checking and answering customers.
As the **most junior** person on the most automatable job, I'm near the top of the list.
do: Ask my team leader **this month** about trainee work on the complex claims team.
Use the **summary tool** daily so I look as fast as the colleagues who already do.
Grow savings from **four to six months** and drop weekend trips.
feel: A **tight chest** about being an easy cut.
**Angry** that savings for the company get dressed up as our luck.
S1.quote: Insurers won't sack clerks in that world. They'll just quietly stop hiring juniors like me.
fieldNote: She **covers both sides**: collective protection out loud, quiet self-protection at her desk.
She worries more for a **weaker colleague** than herself, which says a lot about her values.
Her read of exposure is **sharp and specific**: she matched the card's list to her own tasks.

steps.text: Ask team leader Ruth for a trainee spot on complex claims
Push the union branch for a written deal on intake jobs
Use the claim summary tool every day, not now and then
Stop weekend trips and build savings to six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even finish learning the hard claims. There'd be nothing left for me to get good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loudly, and I'd mean it: this needs government stepping in, a proper wage guarantee or a tax on the companies doing it. At the branch I'd want us out on the street, not sending polite emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I think my job is gone within those two years, full stop. A claims desk is pure thinking work on a screen. The only bit of my day that's hands-on is opening the post, and that's not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking at hands-on training straight away, because the card says robots come three years after. I've always thought about dental nursing, my cousin does it and the course is about a year. I'd cut everything back, keep Tomas's wage for rent and put mine in the bank while I still had it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's going. I'd be lying awake doing the maths on the bedroom ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots come three years after. What does that mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The difference is Tomas. A bus driver is hands-on, so if the card's right, he's got about three years longer than me. So for a while it'd be his wage paying the rent and mine going into savings, and then after that I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest conversation at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the deposit to go into a course instead, which would be a fight. We've talked about that flat for two years. Telling my partner Tomas that the deposit pays for my dental nursing course is the conversation I'd dread.

say: I'd demand **government step in** with a wage guarantee or a tax on the firms.
I'd want the union branch **out on the street**, not sending polite emails.
think: My claims desk is **gone within two years**, because it's all screen work.
My partner's **bus job** buys our household about three extra years.
do: Enrol in a **dental nursing course**, about a year long, within months.
Pay rent from my partner's wage and **bank all of mine**.
Join any **union protest** on job guarantees right away.
feel: Like the **floor's going**, doing sums on the ceiling at night.
S2.quote: A claims desk is pure thinking work on a screen. The only bit of my day that's hands-on is opening the post, and that's not a career.
fieldNote: She immediately **separated thinking from hands-on** work and saw her job sits entirely on the wrong side.
The **three-year robot gap** matters only through her partner's job, not her own.
The real loss she fears is the **flat deposit**, which carries their plans together.

steps.text: Enrol in a one-year dental nursing course within months
Bank her whole wage and live on her partner's bus pay
March with the union for wage guarantees from government

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but it's long enough to actually do something instead of just panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before, but with a deadline: we have five years, so let's get the retraining money agreed now. I'd write to my local representative, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the desk job still goes, it just goes later. I'd have time to finish the dental nursing course properly, part-time, and still earn while I do it. I'm not great at claims anyway, so honestly it's a push I might need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the part-time course next September and do it over two years in the evenings. I'd keep working at Harbourline, take the shadowing, keep the savings going, and push the union for paid study leave. Tomas and I might still buy the flat, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but not frozen. Five years feels like a plan and two years feels like a fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave claims if you had the time to choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I would. I'd rather have a job with my hands in someone's mouth than a job a computer can do better in three seconds. My mum would laugh at that sentence, but I mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What year would be hardest in that five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the year when everyone around me starts leaving. Some will go into the AI checking jobs, some will just get let go. I'd be the one with the evening course and bags under my eyes.

say: I'd ask for **retraining money** to be agreed now, while there's still five years.
I'd write to my **local representative** for the first time in my life.
think: The desk job **still goes**, just later, which gives me time to finish a course.
Being **not great at claims** makes the push easier to accept.
do: Start a **part-time** dental nursing course next September, over two years.
Push the union for **paid study leave** while staying at Harbourline.
Keep saving and consider a **smaller flat** with my partner.
feel: **Nervous** but not frozen; five years feels like a plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather have a job with my hands in someone's mouth than a job a computer can do better in three seconds.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her from **reactive to planning**; the same course becomes a part-time choice.
She frames leaving claims as a **relief**, not a loss, which fits her weak fit for the job.
She shifts from protest to **lobbying** once there's time to use normal channels.

steps.text: Start an evening dental nursing course next September
Write to her local representative about retraining money
Keep saving monthly but look at a smaller flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole other life, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be calmer saying it: we've got ten years, so let's do this properly, with real training schemes and not just a leaflet. I'd keep going to the union meetings, but I wouldn't be shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I might stay in claims for a few years and get good at the new tools first. There'd probably be jobs checking what the AI decides, at least for a while. Then around thirty-two or so I'd move into something hands-on before it closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Harbourline, take every course they offer on the AI system, and try to get onto the team that checks its decisions. I'd keep saving and we'd probably buy the flat. Then I'd do dental nursing or something like it later, maybe paid for by the company if the union wins that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit uneasy, because ten years goes fast when you're paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about plans outside work, like a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids, maybe. We've said maybe at thirty. With ten years, I'd still have them, I think, but I'd want to be in the new job before, not during.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk of having this much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. With ten years I'd be tempted to put it off, and then it'd be year eight and I'd be the oldest junior on the claims floor.

say: I'd ask calmly for **real training schemes**, not just a leaflet.
I'd keep going to **union meetings**, without the shouting.
think: I could **stay in claims** and learn the new tools for a few years.
There may be **checking jobs** reviewing AI decisions, but only for a while.
do: Take every **AI system course** Harbourline offers and aim for the checking team.
Keep saving and **buy the flat** with my partner.
Plan a move into **hands-on work** around age thirty-two.
feel: Mostly okay, a little **uneasy** that ten years goes fast on rent.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd be tempted to put it off, and then it'd be year eight and I'd be the oldest junior on the claims floor.
fieldNote: With a decade, she **chooses to stay** and learn the tools before switching.
She knows her own **procrastination risk** and names it unprompted.
**Family timing** comes up only in this scenario, once the pressure eases.

steps.text: Take every Harbourline course on the new AI claims system
Buy a small flat with her partner Tomas
Plan a switch into dental nursing around age thirty-two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to learn anything new while you're paying rent. What would help is paid retraining you can do while you still earn, and a guarantee from the company that intake staff get first pick of the new roles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who teaches us. Everyone talks about AI taking jobs, but nobody has time to train juniors now, never mind then. If you want young people to survive this, somebody has to sit next to us and show us the hard claims.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI taking jobs, but nobody has time to train juniors now, never mind then.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** motor claims intake clerk at Harbourline, fourteen months in and below target.
She lives with her partner, a **bus driver**, with about four months saved towards a flat deposit.
A **union member**, she backs collective action but quietly works to stay useful herself.
As the scenarios speed up, she moves from **shadowing seniors** to planning dental nursing as a hands-on fallback.
Her deepest complaint is that **no one trains** juniors, with or without AI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain while paying rent.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while still earning, and first pick of new roles for intake staff.
